correctness.rationale: The leaf deletion in a strip of width at most three is a sequence of valid closed-neighborhood dominations. In width three, the two endpoint leaf copies are dominated by the middle parent copy; after those deletions the middle leaf copy is also dominated by it. In width two the opposite parent copy dominates each leaf copy in the specified order; in width one the parent suffices. Distances of surviving vertices are unchanged. For n≥7, the common radius-two neighborhoods of columns at distance two give exactly the intervening three consecutive columns, so the cover catches every simplex. Its nonempty intersections are strips of widths one, two or three; the nerve consists of consecutive triples and their faces, with a unique triangle incident on each distance-two edge. The resulting collapse proves S¹. The cellular product C_n×T has the scale-one graph as its 1-skeleton and one 2-cell per square. Its H₂=0 and H₁=Z imply the square boundaries are independent and primitive in the graph cycle lattice. Each square spans a tetrahedron in X₂, and the projection to the cycle Rips complex and any fixed-tree-coordinate section show that an ordinary rim cycle maps to a generator. This proves the exact split integral kernel. At n=6 with T a point the clique complex is the octahedral boundary. The frozen checks report 20 finite cases with mod-two homology, not an integral or universal proof; the support was inspected, not executed.

evidence: Theorem 3.11 gives a homotopy equivalence from the union of the two Rips complexes along the common Rips complex to the Rips complex of the metric gluing, when each diameter-bounded simplex meeting both outside parts has a unique nonempty maximal extension in A.

In this leaf gluing, any cross simplex must have all outside vertices in one column i, all one tree edge from p. Indeed, opposite-side distances already cost at least two in the tree. Its entire allowable subset in A is the closed radius-one cycle neighborhood of i at height p; it is nonempty and has diameter at most two. It is the required unique maximal extension.
broader_coverage.reasoning: Theorem 3.11 applies directly at the inclusive scale (or at any strict scale between 2 and 3 for these integer distances). All inclusions are simplicial cofibrations. Gluing on the prism along a rim inclusion that is a homotopy equivalence preserves the old homotopy type. Remove leaves to reach the one-vertex fiber. This is actual coverage, not just a resemblance to path gluing. Hypercube results are a different family and are not used to obtain coverage.

originality.rationale: The exact arbitrary-tree wording was not located independently, but its homotopy conclusion follows by direct iteration of the published metric-gluing theorem of Adamaszek et al., Theorem 3.11, with the already established circular-ladder prism result. The gluing applies along an entire rim, not merely a point or short path. Its unique-maximal-common-simplex condition is automatic for a leaf-edge gluing at radius two. The integral conclusion then follows from the cellular product cycle quotient and from filling its squares. The alternative strip-and-nerve proof is correct but does not leave a distinct finding as written.
residual_risks: An earlier source explicitly naming arbitrary tree fibers could exist; exact historical priority is not needed for the coverage decision.
The published gluing theory was compared on its decisive theorem, not on every product-metric discussion in the paper.

value.rationale: A tree-fiber persistence computation is a natural question, and the strip proof is a useful explanation. But the stated homotopy type already follows from the finite metric gluing criterion and the known prism case by leaf induction, and the stated kernel follows routinely from the usual product cellular boundary. The finding does not claim a new structural feature beyond those consequences, such as a distinct scale regime or a stronger map or collapse theorem.
